title: Git Basics
description: Install, configure, and start working with Git repositories

comicStory.title: The New Job Chaos

panels.text: Day 1 at new company. Boss says: 'Copy project files from shared drive.'
You copy 5GB of files manually. Takes forever. Files are outdated!
No idea what changed recently. Start working, accidentally delete important file.
No way to recover! Panic mode activated!
TWIST: Colleague shows you Git. 'Just run: git clone <url>'
Get complete project + full history in seconds! Make mistakes? Revert easily! Always in sync!

comicStory.twist: Manual file copying is chaos. Git clone gets you everything instantly!
comicStory.lesson: Git Basics = Your entry ticket to professional development!

deepDive.whatItIs: Git Basics are the foundational steps to install Git, configure your identity, create or copy repositories, and start tracking changes. It's like setting up your workspace and learning the essential tools.
deepDive.whyItMatters: Without proper Git setup, you can't track changes, collaborate with teams, or use modern development workflows. Git basics are the entry point to professional software development and data engineering.
whereUsed: Starting new projects: Use git init to create repository
Joining existing projects: Use git clone to copy from GitHub
Daily development: Use git status to track changes
Team collaboration: Configure identity for commit tracking
All development environments: Windows, macOS, Linux

Verify: git --version

visualExamples.title: git init vs git clone
visualExamples.description: Two ways to start with Git
visualExamples.diagram:
git init:
- Start NEW project
- Create repository locally
- Use: mkdir project && cd project && git init

git clone:
- Join EXISTING project
- Copy from remote (GitHub)
- Use: git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git

visualExamples.title: git status
visualExamples.diagram:
Shows:
✔ Current branch
✔ Modified files (red)
✔ Staged files (green)
✔ Untracked files
✔ What needs to be committed

keyPoints: Install Git first: Download from git-scm.com or use package manager
Configure identity: git config --global user.name and user.email
git init: Creates new repository (for new projects)
git clone: Copies existing repository (for joining projects)
git status: Shows current state (use frequently!)
.git folder: Contains all repository data (never delete!)
Git works locally without GitHub (Git ≠ GitHub)

interactiveQA.question: What is the first step to use Git?
interactiveQA.explanation: Download Git from git-scm.com (Windows), use Homebrew on macOS, or apt-get on Linux. Verify with 'git --version'. Without installation, you can't use Git commands!

interactiveQA.question: Why configure username and email?
interactiveQA.explanation: Git needs to know who you are. Every commit includes author name and email, which shows in history and helps track who made what changes. Required for collaboration!

interactiveQA.question: What does git init do?
interactiveQA.explanation: Initializes a new repository in your current folder, creating a .git directory. Use for NEW projects. Example: mkdir my-project && cd my-project && git init

interactiveQA.question: What does git clone do?
interactiveQA.answer: Copies an existing repository from remote.
interactiveQA.explanation: Downloads complete project with full history from GitHub/GitLab. Use for EXISTING projects. Example: git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git

interactiveQA.question: What's the difference between git init and git clone?
interactiveQA.answer: init creates new project, clone copies existing project.
interactiveQA.explanation: Use git init when starting YOUR new project. Use git clone when joining EXISTING project from GitHub. init = new, clone = copy.

interactiveQA.question: What does git status show?
interactiveQA.answer: Current state of repository and files.
interactiveQA.explanation: Shows: current branch, modified files, staged files, untracked files, and what needs to be committed. Use frequently to know what's happening!

codingChallenge.title: Git Basics Workflow
codingChallenge.scenario: You're starting a new data engineering project. Simulate the Git initialization workflow: create repository, configure user, create files, and check status.
codingChallenge.problem: Create a class that simulates Git initialization, configuration, file creation, and status checking.
codingChallenge.expectedOutput:
Initialized repository: my-project
Configured user: Ankit Kumar <ankit@example.com>
Created file: README.md
Status: 1 untracked file
hints: Create a GitRepository class with init, config, create_file, and status methods
Track initialized state, user info, and files
Status should show untracked files (not yet tracked by Git)
Simulate the workflow: init → config → create file → status
codingChallenge.solution:
class GitRepository:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.initialized = False
        self.user_name = None
        self.user_email = None
        self.files = []
        self.tracked_files = []
    
    def init(self):
        self.initialized = True
        print(f"Initialized repository: {self.name}")
    
    def config(self, name, email):
        self.user_name = name
        self.user_email = email
        print(f"Configured user: {name} <{email}>")
    
    def create_file(self, filename):
        self.files.append(filename)
        print(f"Created file: {filename}")
    
    def status(self):
        untracked = [f for f in self.files if f not in self.tracked_files]
        print(f"Status: {len(untracked)} untracked file(s)")
        for f in untracked:
            print(f"  - {f}")

# Usage
repo = GitRepository("my-project")
repo.init()
repo.config("Ankit Kumar", "ankit@example.com")
repo.create_file("README.md")
repo.status()
codingChallenge.explanation: This simulates Git basics: init() creates repository, config() sets user identity, create_file() adds files, status() shows untracked files. In real Git: git init, git config, touch file, git status.

quiz.question: What's the first step to use Git?
quiz.explanation: You must install Git first. Download from git-scm.com, install, and verify with 'git --version'. Without installation, Git commands won't work.

quiz.question: Why configure username and email in Git?
quiz.explanation: Git needs your identity because every commit records who made the change. This shows in history and is required for collaboration. Use: git config --global user.name and user.email

quiz.question: What does 'git init' do?
quiz.explanation: git init initializes a new repository in your current folder, creating a .git directory. Use for NEW projects you're starting from scratch.

quiz.question: What does 'git clone' do?
quiz.explanation: git clone copies an existing repository from remote (like GitHub) to your local machine, including full history. Use for EXISTING projects you're joining.

quiz.question: Difference between 'git init' and 'git clone'?
options: init = new project, clone = copy existing
quiz.explanation: git init starts a NEW project locally. git clone copies an EXISTING project from remote. Use init for your projects, clone for others' projects.

quiz.question: What does 'git status' show?
options: Current state of repository and files
quiz.explanation: git status shows: current branch, modified files, staged files, untracked files, and what needs to be committed. Use frequently to understand repository state!

quiz.question: How often should you run 'git status'?
quiz.explanation: Run git status frequently: before committing, after making changes, when unsure about state. It's free, instant, and helps you understand what's happening!

quiz.question: What is the .git folder?
options: Contains all Git repository data and history
quiz.explanation: The .git folder stores all commits, history, and configuration. Created by git init. NEVER delete this folder - you'll lose all history!

quiz.question: Can you use Git without GitHub?
options: Yes, Git works locally without GitHub
quiz.explanation: Git is a local version control tool that works without internet. GitHub is a hosting platform for remote repositories. Git ≠ GitHub!
